q: Before going onto cardiopulmonary bypass, what heparin dose and ACT target are used?
why: Heparin 300–400 u/kg (corrected body weight) aiming for ACT above 400–480 s (normal 80–120 s) or 3× baseline, rechecked every 30 minutes.

q: After 400 u/kg heparin, the ACT is only 260 s. The patient has been on a heparin infusion for a week. What is the most likely cause?
why: Heparin resistance (around 20% of CPB cases) is most commonly due to antithrombin III deficiency, congenital or acquired (prolonged heparin, liver failure, renal loss, DIC). Treat with antithrombin concentrate or FFP.

q: How does high-potassium cardioplegia protect the myocardium?
o: It arrests the heart in systole
It arrests the heart in diastole by preventing repolarisation
It lowers the heart rate to around 30/min
why: Raised K+ arrests the heart in diastole, cutting myocardial oxygen demand. Mg2+ is antiarrhythmic, low Ca2+ reduces contraction, bicarbonate buffers acidosis and mannitol reduces oedema.

q: A patient with severe aortic regurgitation is having CABG on bypass. How is cardioplegia best delivered?
o: Antegrade into the aortic root only
It is not needed in aortic regurgitation
why: Antegrade delivery via the aortic root needs adequate root pressure and a competent aortic valve. With significant AR, cardioplegia runs into the LV, so retrograde via the coronary sinus is used.

q: During hypothermic bypass, which acid–base strategy best preserves cerebral autoregulation in an adult?
why: Alpha-stat does not correct for temperature, allowing relative alkalosis during cooling and preserving autoregulation. pH-stat adds CO2, causing cerebral vasodilation and loss of autoregulation.

q: On cardiopulmonary bypass the PaCO2 is 6.8 kPa. Which change will lower it?
o: Increase the FiO2 on the oxygenator
Increase the sweep gas flow through the oxygenator
why: In the membrane oxygenator, raising FiO2 raises PaO2 and raising gas (sweep) flow lowers PaCO2. MAP is set by pump flow and SVR.

q: Shortly after protamine is given at the end of bypass, PA pressure rises sharply and systemic BP falls. What is the most likely mechanism?
why: Protamine reactions include systemic hypotension, anaphylactoid reactions and severe pulmonary vasoconstriction with RV failure, as well as bleeding.

q: After CABG with long saphenous vein harvest, a patient reports numbness over the medial lower leg. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why: Peripheral nerve injuries after cardiac surgery include saphenous and infrapatellar injury at vein harvest sites, as well as brachial plexus, ulnar, phrenic and recurrent laryngeal injuries.

q: Which intra-operative measure reduces the risk of neurological injury after cardiac surgery?
o: Rapid rewarming at the end of bypass
Allowing MAP to drift to 40 mmHg on bypass
why: Avoid fast rewarming, maintain CPP and haemodynamic stability, avoid disturbing aortic plaque, control glucose and acid–base, and consider NIRS and BIS.

q: Which haemodynamic goals are appropriate when anaesthetising a patient with severe aortic regurgitation?
o: Fast heart rate, reduced SVR, maintained contractility
High SVR with a phenylephrine infusion
why: “Fast and loose”: a higher heart rate shortens diastole (less regurgitation) and a lower SVR favours forward flow. Maintain contractility and sinus rhythm.
